⟨e⟩ between ⟨g⟩ and a back vowel letter is not a vowel: it only marks the soft [ʒ] of ⟨g⟩ before ⟨a o u⟩. mangeait [mɑ̃ʒɛ], pigeon [piʒɔ̃], bourgeois [buʁʒwa], nageant [naʒɑ̃], geôle [ʒol], George [ʒɔʁʒ]. The same mute ⟨e⟩ stands after ⟨j⟩ in Jean [ʒɑ̃] and Jeanne [ʒan]. Martinon (1913, pp. 164 and 239: the ⟨e⟩ between ⟨g⟩ and ⟨a o u⟩ is not pronounced and only gives ⟨g⟩ its sound before ⟨e i⟩ (mangea, pigeon, nageoire, Georges); p. 164 n. 1: J(e)an, J(e)anne, J(e)annot). ⟨g⟩ itself already reads [ʒ] before ⟨e⟩ (before_front_vowel). RESIDUAL: ⟨geu⟩ before ⟨r⟩ in gageure, mangeure and vergeure is [ʒy] (Martinon 1913: 240), but the tokenizer reads ⟨eu⟩ as one grapheme there, so the rule cannot reach it.

The ⟨e⟩ of a word-final ⟨-ied⟩ is close-mid [e], not the [ɛ] of FR_E_CLOSED_FINAL: pied [pje], sied [sje], assied, trépied, marchepied. Martinon (1913, p. 53: the final ⟨e⟩ of pied, sied, messied and assied is close [e]).
FR_IED_CLOSE_MID behind the silent plural ⟨-s⟩: pieds [pje], trépieds. Martinon (1913, p. 53: the final ⟨e⟩ of pied, sied, messied and assied is close [e]).

The two exceptions Martinon names to the mute e of re- before ⟨ss⟩ have a close [e]: ressusciter [ʁesysite] and its forms, because the word comes straight from Latin resuscitare and not from French susciter, and ressuyer, made from essuyer. Martinon (1913, p. 171); Lexique 3.83 ressusciter [ʁesysite]. Ordered before FR_E_MUTE_PREFIX_RE_SS. Like FR_P_MUTE_COMPT, the condition names the word family by its spelling with word_contains_grapheme, because the letters re-ss-u do not decide it (ressurgir keeps [ʁə], Lexique 3.83). The forms of ressuyer with ⟨ui⟩ (ressuie, ressuies, ressuient, ressuiera) are matched by ⟨ressuie⟩: TLFi, s.v. ressuyer, gives [ʁesɥije] and (il) ressuie [-sɥi]. The noun ressui, which Lexique 3.83 reads [ʁəsɥi], is not matched.

Identity rule ordered before FR_E_BEFORE_DOUBLED_NONFINAL: the prefix re- keeps its mute ⟨e⟩ before ⟨ss⟩, which only keeps the ⟨s⟩ voiceless: ressembler [ʁəsɑ̃ble], ressentir, resserrer, ressortir, ressource. Martinon (1913, p. 171: ⟨e⟩ before a doubled consonant letter is not a mute e, with the exceptions dessus, dessous and the prefix re- before ⟨ss⟩ (ressembler, ressentir, resserrer, ressort, ressource), where the ⟨ss⟩ only keeps the ⟨s⟩ voiceless; p. 151 n. 1 says the same of re- and of dessus and dessous). Martinon also names ressusciter and ressuyer as exceptions with [e]; FR_E_RESSUSCITER_RESSUYER, ordered before this rule, reads them. dessus and dessous, the other exception he names, are whole-word entries. cresson and cressonnière, where Martinon (1913: 171) keeps the mute e 'at least at Paris', are whole-word entries too.

⟨e⟩ before a doubled consonant letter in a syllable before the last is not a schwa: message [mesaʒ], dessert [desɛʁ], dessin, cesser [sese], serrer [seʁe], terrible [teʁibl], nettoyer [netwaje], effet [efɛ], effort. Martinon (1913, p. 171: ⟨e⟩ before a doubled consonant letter is not a mute e, with the exceptions dessus, dessous and the prefix re- before ⟨ss⟩ (ressembler, ressentir, resserrer, ressort, ressource), where the ⟨ss⟩ only keeps the ⟨s⟩ voiceless; p. 151 n. 1 says the same of re- and of dessus and dessous). Martinon does not fix the quality of this unstressed vowel; the rule writes [e], the reading of the wikipron fr gold in 500 of the 591 word-initial types (ss 190 [e] against 12 [ɛ] once the re- types are set apart, rr 197 against 13, ll 69 against 27, tt 35 against 21, ff 6 against 4). ⟨nn⟩ and ⟨mm⟩ stay out: there ⟨e⟩ is often the nasal prefix en- (ennui [ɑ̃nɥi], emmener).

FR_E_BEFORE_DOUBLED_CONSONANT for ⟨ss ff pp cc⟩: in the last syllable the ⟨e⟩ before them is open [ɛ], messe [mɛs], presse, jeunesse [ʒœnɛs], greffe [ɡʁɛf], steppe. Martinon (1913, p. 59: the open e of -esse in nièce, vieillesse, noblesse, allégresse, and of -effe in greffe).

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant. A single letter spelling a consonant CLUSTER closes the syllable by itself (⟨x⟩ = /ks/: Alexandre [alɛksɑ̃dʁ]) — Tranel 1987 §4; Walker 2001.

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant.

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant.

Loi de position for /ɔ/ (Tranel 1987 §3): mid back vowel is close [o] in a word-final open syllable (mot [mo], numéro) and before /z/ (rose [ʁoz], chose); open [ɔ] in other closed syllables (bord, botte).

Loi de position for /ɔ/ (Tranel 1987 §3): mid back vowel is close [o] in a word-final open syllable (mot [mo], numéro) and before /z/ (rose [ʁoz], chose); open [ɔ] in other closed syllables (bord, botte).

⟨au⟩ is [ɔ], not its usual [o], before /ʁ/: Laure [lɔʁ], aurore [ɔʁɔʁ], restaurant [ʁɛstɔʁɑ̃], Aurélie [ɔʁeli], dinosaure [dinozɔʁ]. This is the one systematic exception to the otherwise exceptionless ⟨au⟩ = [o] of the loi de position, and it is stated as such by Fouché (1959), Traité de prononciation française, for ⟨au⟩ + r, by Tranel (1987), The Sounds of French, ch. 3, and by Walker (2001), French Sound Structure, ch. 3, all of which name /ʁ/ as an opening environment for the mid back vowel in standard (Parisian/northern) French. Modelled as Parisian, which is what the wikipron gold transcribes; a southern speaker generalises close [o] much more widely and would not want this rule. Residual counter-examples are learned or foreign (Saurat, nauruan, vaurien), where the spelling is not a native ⟨aur⟩ sequence.

⟨eu⟩ stays close-mid [ø] before /z/ even though the syllable is closed — Deleuze [dəløz], yeuz [jøz] — the front-rounded counterpart of the ⟨o⟩ rule FR_O_BEFORE_Z above (rose [ʁoz], chose). /z/ is the standard closing-environment exception to the loi de position, named as such by Fouché (1959), Traité de prononciation française, by Tranel (1987), The Sounds of French, §3, and by Walker (2001), French Sound Structure, ch. 3, which lists it for the whole mid series and not for the back vowel alone. Most French ⟨euse⟩ words (heureuse, creuse, chanteuse) already reach [ø] without this rule, because their mute ⟨e⟩ and mute-word-final ⟨s⟩ strip back to an open syllable; this rule covers the residue where the /z/ is spelled ⟨z⟩ and so is not strippable.

⟨c⟩ before ⟨œu⟩ is hard [k] (cœur [kœʁ], écœurer), although ⟨œ⟩ is a front vowel letter: ⟨œu⟩ is the native ⟨eu⟩ vowel written with an ⟨o⟩ that imitates the Latin spelling, and a ⟨c⟩ before it stays [k]. Before a bare ⟨œ⟩, which is Greek ⟨οι⟩, ⟨c⟩ softens as before ⟨é⟩ (cœlacanthe [selakɑ̃t]). French orthography, Wikipedia: after ⟨c⟩, ⟨œ⟩ gives [k] in some words (cœur) and [s] in others (cœlacanthe), and the [s] reading is the one before ⟨æ⟩ and ⟨œ⟩ in scientific terms of Latin and Greek origin. ⟨ch⟩ before ⟨œu⟩ in chœur [kœʁ] is FR_CH_HARD_BEFORE_OEU (Martinon 1913: 222). Stated as a rule on ⟨c⟩, not as a ⟨cœu⟩ key: a ⟨cœu⟩ key would pass none of the three key tests, because its value [kœ] is the concatenation of a hard ⟨c⟩ and ⟨œu⟩. Source: TLFi chœur, Prononc. [kœ:ʀ], 'Homon. cœur', so cœur is [kœ:ʀ] too (cnrtl.fr/definition/chœur; saved in Papers/Languages/Romance/French/cnrtl_choeur.html).

Word-final ⟨ai⟩ with nothing following is close-mid /e/ (⟨j'ai⟩ [ʒe], ⟨vrai⟩ [vʁe], ⟨quai⟩ [ke]), against open-mid /ɛ/ whenever a consonant letter follows it (⟨mais⟩ [mɛ], ⟨lait⟩ [lɛ]) — the loi de position stated for the last syllable of the word (Walker 2001; Fouché 1959).

⟨e⟩ before a doubled ⟨ll⟩, ⟨tt⟩ or ⟨rr⟩ in the last syllable of the word stands in a word-final closed syllable and is [ɛ], not schwa: elle [ɛl], cette [sɛt], belle [bɛl], terre [tɛʁ], guerre [ɡɛʁ] (Féry 2001: 8, ex. (19) 'Only [ɛ] in word-final closed syllables', with elle and cette among the examples, and generalisation (20b) 'No [e], but always [ɛ] before a final consonant'). followed_by_nucleus false keeps the rule to that syllable. The same closure is why ⟨ll tt rr⟩ stay one consonant. Lexique 3.83 (New et al. 2004) reads this ⟨e⟩ as [ɛ] in 1476 of the 1478 word types that end in -elle(s), -ette(s) or -erre(s); the other two are moelle and moelles [mwal], where ⟨oe⟩ spells one vowel. NOT MODELLED: the same ⟨e⟩ in an earlier syllable. Féry states the generalisation for word-final syllables only, and Lexique reads that ⟨e⟩ as [ɛ] in some words (terrible, tellement) and as [e] in others (cellule, nettoyer, serrer), so no rule here covers it. ⟨ss ff nn mm⟩ are left out: the prefixes de- and re- end with a schwa before ⟨ss⟩ (dessus [dəsy], ressembler [ʁəsɑ̃ble]), and ⟨mm⟩ after ⟨e⟩ can spell [a] (femme [fam]).

⟨x⟩ of a word-initial ⟨ex⟩ before a vowel letter is [ɡz]: exemple [ɛɡzɑ̃pl], exercice, exister [ɛɡziste], exiger, exotique, examen, exact. Martinon (1913, pp. 348-349: before a vowel, initial ex- (or hex-) is regularly [ɡz] (exalter, exhaler, exécuter, exiger, exotique, exubérant) and so are its derivatives (inexigible, inexact); p. 347: elsewhere inside a word ⟨x⟩ is [ks] (laxatif, maxime, sexuel)). Martinon notes that exécration and exécrable are often said with [ks] for emphasis; they take the rule.

FR_X_VOICED_INITIAL_EX before a mute ⟨h⟩: exhiber [ɛɡzibe], exhaler, exhaustif. Martinon (1913, pp. 348-349: before a vowel, initial ex- (or hex-) is regularly [ɡz] (exalter, exhaler, exécuter, exiger, exotique, exubérant) and so are its derivatives (inexigible, inexact); p. 347: elsewhere inside a word ⟨x⟩ is [ks] (laxatif, maxime, sexuel)).

FR_X_VOICED_INITIAL_EX after a vowel-final prefix, the derivatives Martinon names: coexister [kɔɛɡziste], réexaminer, préexistant. In these spellings a vowel letter before ⟨ex⟩ marks the prefix boundary; all 86 such types of the wikipron fr gold have [ɡz]. Martinon (1913, pp. 348-349: before a vowel, initial ex- (or hex-) is regularly [ɡz] (exalter, exhaler, exécuter, exiger, exotique, exubérant) and so are its derivatives (inexigible, inexact); p. 347: elsewhere inside a word ⟨x⟩ is [ks] (laxatif, maxime, sexuel)). RESIDUAL: after the consonant-final prefix in- (inexact, inexistant) the rule cannot see the word start three slots back, so ⟨x⟩ stays [ks]; hex- (Hexagone) is not reached either.

⟨x⟩ before the ordinal ⟨-ième⟩ is [z], the liaison consonant of deux, six and dix: deuxième [døzjɛm], sixième [sizjɛm], dixième [dizjɛm]. Martinon (1913, p. 348: deuxième, dixième, sixième have the [z] of the liaison of deux, six, dix). The condition on a consonant two slots back keeps out the letter name in ixième [iksjɛm] (wikipron fr).

⟨g⟩ before ⟨t⟩ is mute: vingt [vɛ̃], vingtaine [vɛ̃tɛn], vingtième, doigt [dwa], doigté, longtemps [lɔ̃tɑ̃]. Martinon (1913, p. 236: ⟨g⟩ is mute in vin(gt) and its derivatives, lon(g)temps and doi(gt)). Every native ⟨gt⟩ type of the wikipron fr gold agrees; the foreign names Washington and Pingtung keep [ŋt] there and are lexical.

Word-final ⟨g⟩ after a nasal spelling is mute, also behind the silent plural ⟨-s⟩: long [lɔ̃], longs, sang [sɑ̃], rang, étang [etɑ̃], hareng [aʁɑ̃], poing [pwɛ̃], coing, seing. Martinon (1913, p. 236: at the end of a French word ⟨g⟩ is not pronounced; it survives in the spelling after a nasal: ran(g), san(g), étan(g), haren(g), sein(g), coin(g), poin(g), lon(g)). Martinon (1913: 238) gives the pronounced final ⟨g⟩ of foreign words (gong, ginseng, iceberg, the English -ing); the open class of loans in ⟨-ang⟩ and ⟨-ong⟩ (gang, slang, boomerang, mustang) keeps [ɡ] in the wikipron fr gold and is lexical, the same residual as the loanwords in ⟨-er⟩.

⟨ch⟩ before /l ʁ m n/ is [k]: chrétien [kʁetjɛ̃], Christ, chronologie, chrome, chlore [klɔʁ], technique [tɛknik], drachme. Martinon (1913, p. 226: before a consonant ⟨ch⟩ is always learned and keeps the velar sound; the consonants are the liquids and nasals l, m, n, r, and sometimes s and t (chlore, drachme, technique, chrétien)). The rule takes only the four consonants Martinon names without restriction; before ⟨s⟩ and ⟨t⟩ he says only 'parfois', and fichtre keeps [ʃ]. The German loan families chlinguer, chnoque and chleuh keep [ʃ] in every form (Lexique 3.83: chlinguer [ʃlɛ̃ɡe], chlingues [ʃlɛ̃ɡ], chnoques [ʃnɔk], chleuhs [ʃlø]), so word_contains_grapheme_not names their spellings; whole-word entries would miss the conjugated and inflected forms.

⟨ch⟩ before ⟨œu⟩ is [k]: chœur [kœʁ], chœurs. Martinon (1913, p. 222: co is said in all the words that begin with chol- and chor-, choléra, chorus, choral, 'avec c(h)œur, et leurs dérivés'). The ⟨œu⟩ is the native vowel written with the ⟨o⟩ of the Latin chorus, as in cœur, whose ⟨c⟩ FR_C_HARD_BEFORE_OEU keeps hard. The words in chol- and chor- are not stated: Cholet keeps [ʃ].

⟨p⟩ of a word-final ⟨-mpt⟩ is mute, as the ⟨t⟩ is: prompt [pʁɔ̃], exempt [ɛɡzɑ̃], rompt [ʁɔ̃], corrompt, interrompt. Martinon (1913, p. 129: exempt, prompt, rompt end in the nasal vowel; p. 331: in ⟨-empt⟩ and ⟨-ompt⟩ neither p nor t sounds).

The ⟨p⟩ of the word family of compter is mute: compte [kɔ̃t], compter, comptable, comptoir, décompte, escompte, acompte, recompter. Martinon (1913, p. 285: p is mute in com(p)te and all its derivatives, com(p)tabilité included, but not in exemption, présomption, consomption or symptôme). This is a fact of one word family, not of the letters ⟨mpt⟩: the same letters keep [p] in somptueux, symptôme, présomption and péremptoire, so the condition names the family's spelling ⟨compt⟩ with word_contains_grapheme. Every ⟨compt⟩ type of the wikipron fr gold (about 130) has the mute [p]. Martinon also lists the derivatives of prompt and, with hesitation, dompter, but the gold splits on prompte, promptitude and dompter, and impromptu keeps [p], so those stay out.

The ⟨g⟩ of the English final ⟨-ing⟩ is part of [ŋ] and adds no [ɡ]. Fougeron & Smith (1993: 74-75) transcribe parking [paʁkiŋ] and state that the velar nasal occurs only word-finally in borrowed, usually English, words.

After ⟨gu⟩, ⟨eil⟩ and ⟨eill⟩ spell [œj], the ⟨ueil⟩ of accueil written with the ⟨u⟩ of ⟨gu⟩: orgueil [ɔʁɡœj], enorgueillir. Martinon (1913, p. 93: in ⟨-cueil⟩ and ⟨-gueil⟩ the ⟨ue⟩ is the vowel eu, the u needed by ⟨c⟩ or ⟨g⟩ standing for the second u (accueil, écueil, cercueil, orgueil)). ⟨cueil⟩ needs no rule, because the tokenizer reads its ⟨ueil⟩ as one grapheme.

⟨gu⟩ before ⟨ë⟩ keeps its ⟨u⟩ as [y]: ambiguë [ɑ̃biɡy], ciguë [siɡy], aiguë, contiguë, exiguë. Martinon (1913, p. 241: the ⟨u⟩ of ⟨gu⟩ is pronounced before the mute final ⟨ë⟩ of aiguë, ambiguë, contiguë, exiguë, besaiguë and ciguë).

The ⟨ë⟩ after ⟨gu⟩ is the mute final ⟨e⟩ of the feminine; its diaeresis only marks the ⟨u⟩ as a vowel. Martinon (1913, p. 241: the ⟨u⟩ of ⟨gu⟩ is pronounced before the mute final ⟨ë⟩ of aiguë, ambiguë, contiguë, exiguë, besaiguë and ciguë).

⟨g⟩ before ⟨ü⟩ is hard [ɡ]: the 1990 spellings ambigüe, aigüe and cigüe move the diaeresis to the ⟨u⟩ that Martinon (1913: 241) says is pronounced, so ambigüe [ɑ̃biɡy] reads as ambiguë. ⟨ü⟩ counts as a front vowel letter for before_front_vowel, which would otherwise soften the ⟨g⟩.

Word-final ⟨c⟩ after a nasal spelling is mute, also behind the silent plural ⟨-s⟩: blanc [blɑ̃], blancs, banc, flanc, franc [fʁɑ̃], tronc, jonc, vainc [vɛ̃]. Martinon (1913, p. 213: after a nasal vowel final ⟨c⟩ stayed mute: ban(c), blan(c), flan(c), fran(c), vain(c), convain(c), jon(c), ajon(c), tron(c); in donc it is mute in principle and sounds only when the word opens a clause or is stressed (je pense, donc je suis)). donc is a whole-word entry [dɔ̃k], the reading of Lexique 3.83 (d§k): Martinon sounds its ⟨c⟩ when the word opens a clause (je pense, donc je suis), and a word rule cannot see the clause, so the spec keeps the reading that is right in that position. zinc keeps [ɡ] (Martinon 1913: 214 n. 1: 'on devrait tout simplement écrire zing') as a whole-word entry.

⟨x⟩ between ⟨oi⟩ and a vowel is [s]: soixante [swasɑ̃t], soixantaine, soixantième, soixantenaire. Martinon (1913, p. 347: inside a word ⟨x⟩ is [ks] before a vowel (laxatif, maxime), but the simple [s] of the popular pronunciation stands in soixante and its derivatives, where the etymological ⟨x⟩ was put back after the fact, as in six and dix). soixante and its derivatives are the French words with ⟨oix⟩ before a vowel; the wikipron fr gold has [s] in all of them. Martinon names the [s] of Bruxelles, Auxerre and Auxonne too; they are proper names and stay out.

The final ⟨x⟩ of six and dix, silent in other words, is [s]: six [sis], dix [dis]. Martinon (1913, p. 328: the final ⟨t⟩ of huit is pronounced, page huit, le huit mai, huit hommes; p. 345: the final ⟨x⟩ of six and dix is [s], j'en ai six, page dix, le dix août). A rule on the whole word, not a word_exceptions entry, so the other rules and those of a regional variety still read the rest of the word (fr-CA affricates the /d/ of dix). The forms before a consonant and before a vowel are the FR_*_MUTE_BEFORE_CONSONANT and FR_NUMERAL_Z_BEFORE_VOWEL sandhi rules.

The final ⟨t⟩ of huit, silent in other words, is [t]: huit [ɥit]. Martinon (1913, p. 328: the final ⟨t⟩ of huit is pronounced, page huit, le huit mai, huit hommes; p. 345: the final ⟨x⟩ of six and dix is [s], j'en ai six, page dix, le dix août). A rule on the whole word, not a word_exceptions entry, so the other rules and those of a regional variety still read the rest of the word (fr-CA affricates the /d/ of dix). The forms before a consonant and before a vowel are the FR_*_MUTE_BEFORE_CONSONANT and FR_NUMERAL_Z_BEFORE_VOWEL sandhi rules.

⟨x⟩ before a letter that reads [s] (⟨c⟩ before a front vowel, ⟨s⟩) is [k], not [ks]: excellent [ɛksɛlɑ̃], exception [ɛksɛpsjɔ̃], excès [ɛksɛ], exciter [ɛksite], excentrique. Martinon (1913, p. 348: before a hissing consonant, ce or ci or an s, the second half of the x merges with the sound that follows, so ecs is reduced to ec: ec-cellent, ec-centrique, ec-sangue). Before a hard ⟨c⟩ the [ks] stays (excuse [ɛkskyz]).
